en: Was renowned, and was my support.
Born greater than I,
He would plunge into the facing enemy
And cast them into turmoil.
Full of cunning and fierce in wrath,
He was a merciless lion,
A hero protected by the spirits.
Hero Külchoro, my lion,
Was the one Almighty God alone
Had written upon my brow.
His heroism was extraordinary,
His strength beyond measure;
He was both noble and leonine,
Perfect in all twelve limbs.
He was given the name Külchoro;
Surely God alone
Would never create another like him.
His valor was renowned,
His gray-wolf courage plain to see.
We joined when no bigger than thumbs,
United when tiny as lice,
And met when small as ticks.
We encountered each other in childhood;
He was written upon my brow,
And found as my blessing.
This peerless Külchoro,
His gray-wolf courage was unlike any other’s.
We kicked together like colt and yearling,
And quarreled as we suckled at the breast.
I carved him choice fat and fed him;
I had this boy suckle
At my mother Kanykei’s breast.
To enemies who bore us malice
He was a cauldron of bitter brine,
He made ready all his weapons,
And fastened the gold-inlaid battle-axe,
Your uncle’s Joykuma,
Unscabbarded at his side.
The one he would face was Sarybai;
Turning toward Sarybai,
The lion-warrior took the road.
Ready to die if death had come,
He went to meet fearsome, wrathful Sarybai
And test himself face-to-face.
His valor was renowned;
Külchoro climbed the rise.
When he paused and looked intently,
Ill-fated Sarybai
Stood prepared with his battle gear,
The mad brute standing there,
Straining like a blue tiger.
When one looked at his mustache,
It was like nettles filling a ravine.
His eyes were like lumps of coal;
When one looked at his size,
He was as great as half a towering mountain.
He had the majesty of a lion,
As though he could herd
And trample the entire world—
Such was his appearance.
His gray-wolf ferocity was plain;
The one he faced was venom itself.
Among men, none could overcome him;
He was God’s wrath lying in wait.
He fixed his hostile gaze sharply,
A creature who had come seeking conflict.
Such was the hero’s might;
He was truly God’s wrath.
Your enraged infidel
Seemed to await the whole world.
Forest and tree nearly collapsed,
Smoldering beneath his violence.
He had overrun the world—
Such was hero Sarybai.
To every one of those marksmen
He gave abundant provisions,
Armor the sun could not penetrate,
Pounds of gold ornaments,
A horse as payment,
And lavish rewards without stint.
He had the Dangdung Mountains combed,
For mountain goats from Dangdung’s heights,
Cliff goats with thick hides.
Long ago your valiant mother Kanykei
Had the marksmen shoot them,
And, keeping the scorching sun from them,
Had them covered in a white chest.
She had the hides thoroughly cured,
And, so they would be soft and supple,
Had them placed in the bark
Of apple trees from every mountain valley.
She had them tanned and worked,
And ninety skilled youths
Tended them without rest for nine months
And beat them for ninety days.
She had them folded like a serpent’s belly,
And the flawless leather
Stitched with smooth, close seams.
What proved unfit she had ripped apart;
She sent for sharpened steel
And had it poured over every side.
When the kandagai was pulled,
It stretched like flowing water.
When a facing enemy struck it,
The point of his steel was blunted.
It turned out just as intended:
Embers could not pierce it though dry honeysuckle burned,
Nor bullets, however expertly fired.
Its trouser cuffs were embroidered,
And its seams were bound with steel.
It reduced an enemy who came against it
To helpless frustration.
He donned the kandagai,
And slung the Syrbarang gun over his shoulder.
Against the infidel huge as a mountain,
Against that hero Sarybai,
He went forth to provoke battle,
To fight doggedly for six full months,
And grapple in a bloody struggle;
Ready to die if true death had come,
And, if the true God so willed,
To surrender his fly-like soul.
He mounted a courser swift as water;
The wretched defender of his people
Knotted the gray horse’s tail tightly.
He prepared himself in fury
And began the bitter combat.
The lion Choro bound his precious life
As lightly as a single hair and cast it away.
The one charging was Sarybai;
Such was the field of battle.
He did not look around him,
And spared his life not at all.
He did not glance from side to side,
And cared little for his life.
Against the infidel, son of a monster,
Against the hero like a racing camel,
Whose final hour had come,
Against hero Khan Sarybai,
He rode out and made ready.
He drove Surat forward with his thighs,
And took in hand a fearsome spear
With a steel shaft and a keen point.
The one he would face was Sarybai;
Your valiant one spared not his life.
He shouted, “Baabedin!”
And raised the battle cry, “Manas!”
“May God set this deed aright;
My father, Manas the Destroyer,
Protect me upon this path!”
He shouted, “Manas! Manas!”
And called, “One God, Creator of all,
Protect me!”
Now your valiant one attacked.
The other had driven and devoured
The whole wide world.
He had taken heroes of countless kinds,
Taken innocent peoples,
And destroyed many mighty champions,
Yet even then that swine’s
Single belly had not been filled.
Of the mortals upon the earth,
He had left not one alive.
He had turned his face toward conflict;
Everyone who grappled with him
He gulped down like a dragon,
Devouring the whole world.
All four corners of the earth
Had grown feeble, unable to endure
The swine descending upon them.
He awaited whoever faced him;
When he roared in fury,
The black earth trembled
And smoldered through its depths.
In his rage, the mad brute
Would wrench his battle-gear’s mouth aside.
The creature was no son of man;
He would crush the enemy to dust.
Külchoro attacked the mountain-sized dog,
For he was a lion beyond compare.
The one he would fight was Sarybai;
Such was the foe he faced.
Sparing not his renowned life,
Your wretched, valiant kinsman
Faced the infidel huge as a mountain,
The hero in the fullness of his strength,
Who gnawed apart all he encountered
And swallowed every living soul.
No one who came to face him
Had escaped with life.
He came to wreak ruin in combat
And wrest his people
From the hands of a blessed nation.
The lion Choro gathered his courage:
“I shall slaughter you all.
If I do not slay every last champion,
Leave your people destitute,
And wage the fiercest battle;
If I do not break the backs
Of your men who call themselves heroes;
If I do not massacre your people,
Slaughtering every last soul,
Kill your khans,
And leave your women in black mourning;
If I do not spread slaughter to your borders,
Seize your maidens and women as plunder,
And take every single one;
I bristle in my anger,
And swell as vast as a mountain.
My strength seethes and surges;
Today I roar transformed.
I shall crush every one of your villages,
And load all your gold and silver
For transport toward Jelpiniş.
I am enraged and stand rigid;
If I do not spill your blood like water,
Drink your blood like water,
And quench my thirst;
May I strike down your lower demons
And seize all four kinds of livestock.
If I do not cast a chilling lasso
Over Buurul, whom you would never surrender if asked;
If I do not take as plunder
Your maidens who boast of their beauty,
May I die and cease to be Sarybai,
May I sink into darkness as though never born!
This accursed breed
Does not know it is about to die;
We cannot leave it alive;
That swine can never be redeemed.”
When the infidel, son of a monster,
Saw the hero Choro,
His shout split heads,
And his bellow split stones.
With that thick-muscled dog,
He came forth to confront him.
The one-armed gray-maned lion—
The spirit of Manas appeared openly,
Struck alongside him as a companion,
And openly lent him aid.
They rushed to face each other,
Preparing to meet in combat,
To turn each other’s horses’ heads,
Roaring threateningly,
To charge each other head-on
And test a hero’s courage.
If the true God so willed,
Külchoro would surrender his fly-like soul.
Fierce Külchoro
Unleashed his full courage.
Thinking his poor soul already dead,
He bound it to a hair and cast it away.
The one he faced was Sarybai;
He raised the Syr spear
And rode straight toward him.
Sarybai was a mad brute,
